subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Truth About Recycling Rates
description: Learn The Truth About Recycling Rates in one minute.

hook.text: Only 9% of all plastic ever produced has been recycled. Most ended up in landfills or nature.

buildup.text: Recycling rates vary wildly by material. Aluminum is recycled 75% of the time. Plastic barely at all.

discovery.text: Many items thrown in recycling bins are too contaminated or mixed to actually be recycled.

twist.text: The recycling symbol on packaging doesn't mean it will be recycled — just that it's technically possible.

climax.text: Without better sorting technology and markets for recycled material, most recycling is wishful thinking.

punchline.text: That recycling bin is more hopeful than honest.

quiz.question: What percentage of all plastic ever produced has been recycled?

details.summary: Global recycling rates remain far lower than most people assume. Only about 9 percent of all plastic ever produced has been recycled, and actual recycling rates for mixed municipal waste in many countries hover around 20 to 30 percent.
details.whyItMatters: Believing that recycling is solving the waste problem creates false confidence. Honest assessment of recycling rates reveals the urgent need for waste reduction, better systems, and producer responsibility.
takeaways: Only about 9 percent of all plastic ever made has been recycled
Contamination renders much collected recyclable material unusable
Recycling alone cannot solve the waste crisis

faq.question: Why is the plastic recycling rate so low?
faq.answer: There are thousands of plastic types, many of which cannot be economically recycled. Contamination with food or mixed materials degrades quality. Virgin plastic is often cheaper than recycled. Collection infrastructure is limited outside wealthy countries.

faq.question: Which materials are actually recycled at high rates?
faq.answer: Aluminum cans have recycling rates above 70 percent in many countries because recycling aluminum uses 95 percent less energy than producing new metal. Steel and cardboard also recycle well. Glass and some paper grades achieve moderate rates depending on local infrastructure.
